newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed starts political comeback.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed starts political comeback.

text.p: Russia's popular strongman Alexander Lebed began the fight for his political comeback on Friday after being sacked by President Boris Yeltsin for making waves in the Kremlin.

Lebed's dismissal as secretary of Yeltsin's Security Council ends a four-month marriage of convenience between the general and the ailing president, who said he was fed up with Lebed's argumentative character and presidential ambitions.
The Kremlin newspaper Rossiskiye Vesti greeted the sacking with a gleeful pun on Lebed's name, which means swan.
"The swan has flown away," it said in a banner headline.

But other commentators were not so convinced that Lebed's departure would end either the general's career or Russia's problems, which include mass delays in wage payments, a shaky peace in Chechnya and a president laid low with heart problems.
"The swan flew away yesterday. Where will Russia fly tomorrow?" said Komsomolskaya Pravda.
Lebed, who has denied charges by Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov that he was preparing a "creeping coup", warned that Russia was in for a "hot autumn".

He cited discontent in the crumbling army and the future of the Chechnya peace process he sponsored as Yeltsin's envoy to the rebel region. Interfax news agency quoted presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying Lebed's dimissal from this post was only a matter of time.

"I never had a very high opinion of (Yastrzhembsky). After his statement I know the diagnosis -- his brain has melted," Lebed told Reuters, saying it was obvious he had little chance of resuming his work in Chechnya.

"As of yesterday I am no longer a state official... how is it possible to carry out one's duties when you've been deprived of transport, communication and the means of influencing things? How can one set assignments from a sofa in one's living room?"

Rebel leaders in Chechnya, who view the August peace deal as a victory in their 21-month battle with Russia, announced plans on Friday to hold elections in the region on January 27 -- a move sure to upset Moscow, which says it should be consulted.

Lebed, who said after his sacking that he would have a good sleep and then start polishing his political machine for a presidential bid, braved large crowds to pay a visit to the theatre to see the play "Ivan the Terrible".
"I will learn how to rule the state," he said, displaying characteristic cynicism. The 16th century ruler was renowned for his cruelty and ruthlessness.

Before his sacking Lebed clashed with Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who on Friday strengthened his hand when Yeltsin sacked armed forces chief of staff Mikhail Kolesnikov in what appeared to be part of a purge of the ministry's old guard.

Rodionov was quick to support Lebed's sacking and many members of the lower house of parliament, which met on Friday to discuss the political fallout from Lebed's dismissal, joined the establishment's vigorous criticism of the general.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov made clear he had little love for the man who could dent his support in a future poll.
"His "romance' with Boris Yeltsin lasted only two or three months and it was a clear political bargain," Zyuganov said.
Lebed won his place on Yeltsin's team after coming third in the first round of the presidential election.

But since moving into the Kremlin to help Yeltsin win a second term, the paratroop general has clashed with powerful rivals such as presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, who he said was behind Kulikov's bombshell allegations against him.

Parliament called on the leadership to take firm control of the country and, building on its view that Lebed was in bed with Chechnya's rebels, asked for an investigation into anyone who might foment unrest and threaten Russia's territorial integrity.
